common_name: Itasca Grape (Cold-Hardy Low-Acid White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun once soil is workable.

directions: Itasca is a University of Minnesota-bred white wine grape released in 2017, the fifth cultivar from the program's cold-hardy breeding effort, surviving winter lows into USDA Zone 4. Its naturally low acidity and high sugar accumulation set it apart from earlier Minnesota releases like La Crescent, yielding a light straw-colored wine with pear, quince, melon, and violet aromas and a long finish. The vine shows strong field resistance to downy mildew, powdery mildew, and phylloxera, reducing the spray program needed compared to many cold-hardy hybrids. Because clusters ripen with unusually high sugar for a cold-climate grape, growers should monitor for sunburn and manage canopy density to protect fruit quality in hot late-summer stretches.
sources: University of Minnesota Grape Breeding and Enology Program

common_name: Clarion Grape (Cold-Hardy Low-Vigor White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring on a trellis in full sun; performs most reliably in Zone 5 despite marginal Zone 4 hardiness.

directions: Clarion is the University of Minnesota's sixth cold-hardy wine grape release, introduced in 2021 after roughly two decades of breeding work, and shares the aromatic, low-acid style of its sibling Itasca. Compared with older Minnesota-bred hybrids, Clarion grows with noticeably less vigor and produces looser clusters, which eases canopy management and lowers bunch-rot and insect pressure in humid summers. The white wine shows citrus, pear, melon, apricot, and chamomile character, and the vine has demonstrated good resistance to downy mildew in university trials. While bred for Zone 4 cold tolerance, early plantings have performed most consistently in Zone 5 conditions such as Iowa and Wisconsin, so growers in the coldest sites should still watch for winter injury.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Compassion Seedless Grape (Crisp White Table Grape, formerly 'Passion')

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun.

directions: Compassion is a University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture seedless table grape, first released in 2017 under the name Passion and renamed in 2018 to avoid confusion with an unrelated fruit variety of that name. Its white-green berries combine the crisp, thin-skinned bite typical of California table grapes with the richer, fruitier flavor common to eastern American hybrids, a texture combination the breeding program specifically targeted. Vines show good general disease resistance and vine health for the humid South, and fruit is non-slipskin with resistance to cracking after summer rain. As with other Arkansas releases, it is best suited to home gardens and local-market sales rather than long-distance shipping, since fruit softens quickly after harvest.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture

common_name: Faith Seedless Grape (Early Blue Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun.

directions: Faith is a blue-skinned seedless table grape from the University of Arkansas breeding program, one of a quartet released together with Gratitude, Hope, and Joy for local-market growers. It is the earliest-ripening of the four, typically ready in late July to early August, with semi-crisp flesh and a mild, faintly fruity flavor. Like its siblings, the fruit is non-slipskin with good skin quality and resistance to cracking after rain, and the vine has shown solid winter hardiness and general vine health in Arkansas trials. Because berries soften after picking, Faith performs best in dooryard plantings or short local supply chains rather than for extended storage or shipping.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture
International Society for Horticultural Science (Acta Horticulturae)

common_name: Gratitude Seedless Grape (Crisp Green Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun.

directions: Gratitude is a green-skinned seedless table grape from the University of Arkansas breeding program, released alongside its siblings Faith, Hope, and Joy for home garden and local-market use. It stands out among the four for its notably crisp flesh and mild, neutral flavor, and it ripens later than Faith, typically in late August. The berries are non-slipskin with good resistance to cracking, and the vines have shown reliable winter hardiness and general disease tolerance in Arkansas Division of Agriculture trials. Because it was bred for regional and dooryard production rather than commercial shipping, expect smaller clusters and more variable seed remnants than typical grocery-store seedless grapes.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture
International Society for Horticultural Science (Acta Horticulturae)

common_name: Hope Seedless Grape (Soft-Textured Green Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun.

directions: Hope is a green-fruited seedless table grape bred by the University of Arkansas program from a 1983 cross, released together with Faith, Gratitude, and Joy. It carries a pleasantly fruity flavor and a notably soft texture, along with high production potential, ripening in mid-to-late August. The fruit is non-slipskin with good skin quality and resistance to splitting, and the vine has shown dependable winter hardiness and vine health in Arkansas trials. Its soft texture means Hope is best picked and eaten fresh at home or sold through short local-market channels rather than shipped any distance.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture
International Society for Horticultural Science (Acta Horticulturae)

common_name: Joy Seedless Grape (Soft Blue Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun.

directions: Joy is a blue-skinned seedless table grape released by the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, one of four cultivars introduced together with Faith, Gratitude, and Hope for home and local-market growers. It ripens in the first to second week of August and is prized for exceptionally fruity flavor and very thin, tender skin with no noticeable astringency. Like its siblings, Joy is non-slipskin with good resistance to cracking and has shown solid winter hardiness and vine health in university trials. Its very soft texture makes Joy best suited to eating fresh off the vine rather than storage or shipping, so it fits dooryard plantings better than commercial production.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture
International Society for Horticultural Science (Acta Horticulturae)
